convergence: Both responses propose a variable cross-section strategy that adapts the street design to each zone's needs rather than applying a uniform layout. Both allocate two general traffic lanes, two transit/emergency lanes, protected bike lanes, and widened sidewalks across all three zones. Both sequence construction to complete the historically Black neighbourhood first (before the 14-month election), delay the commercial district until last, and position the hospital zone in the middle. Both address the hospital's emergency access concern by designating transit lanes as shared with ambulances and deploying signal priority technology. Both propose side-street parking conversion to offset lost on-street parking in the commercial district. Both recommend establishing a neighbourhood advisory council in Zone 1 and implementing a business support program for the commercial district. Both frame the problem as requiring stakeholder management across equity, safety, commerce, and mobility concerns.

divergences.location: How the construction timeline is divided into phases
divergences.response_a: Divides the 30-month timeline into three phases: Phase 1 (Months 1–10, neighbourhood only), Phase 2 (Months 11–18, hospital only), Phase 3 (Months 19–30, commercial only). Each phase focuses on a single zone.
divergences.response_b: Divides the 30-month timeline into three phases: Phase 1 (Months 1–12, neighbourhood AND hospital transit lanes simultaneously), Phase 2 (Months 13–20, hospital completion AND commercial side-street parking prep), Phase 3 (Months 21–30, commercial only). Each phase combines work across multiple zones.
divergences.nature: Response A sequences zones sequentially with no overlap. Response B sequences zones with partial overlap, running work in multiple zones during the same months. This creates different patterns of construction activity and disruption.
divergences.specificity: Response A specifies exact month ranges for each zone's work (10 months, 7 months, 11 months). Response B specifies month ranges but describes what happens in each zone during overlapping periods (e.g., "hospital completion" while "commercial prep" begins). Response A leaves implicit how long each zone's work takes; Response B makes the overlap explicit but does not specify how many crews or resources are allocated to simultaneous work.

divergences.location: Timing of the hospital zone's construction relative to the election
divergences.response_a: Schedules hospital construction to begin in Month 11, which is after the 14-month election window has closed. The rationale states the city should use the first 10 months to "run simulations and pilot programs with the hospital's medical director to prove the efficacy" before ground is broken.
divergences.response_b: Schedules the hospital's BRT/Emergency lanes to be fully constructed by Month 12, which is before the 14-month election. The rationale states this "proves to the hospital and the public that emergency response times will improve, building trust in the project" during the election cycle.
divergences.nature: Response A treats the hospital construction as something to delay until after the election, using the pre-election period for testing. Response B treats the hospital's transit lanes as something to complete before the election, using the visible completion as political evidence of project viability.
divergences.specificity: Response A specifies what happens during the pre-construction period (simulations and pilots) but does not detail what happens if those pilots reveal problems. Response B does not specify what happens during the pre-construction period; it assumes the lanes can be opened by Month 12 and will demonstrate improved response times immediately.

divergences.location: When side-street parking conversions occur in the commercial district
divergences.response_a: States that the city should "implement the side-street parking conversions *before* the main street parking is removed" but does not specify when this happens within the 30-month timeline. It is presented as a general principle rather than a scheduled action.
divergences.response_b: Explicitly schedules side-street parking conversions to occur during Phase 2 (Months 13–20), before Phase 3 (Months 21–30) when main-street parking is removed. This creates a specific sequence: conversions complete, then main-street construction begins.
divergences.nature: Response A identifies the principle but leaves the timing unscheduled. Response B integrates the parking conversions into the phased timeline as a discrete action with a defined window.
divergences.specificity: Response A leaves open when the conversions happen and whether they are part of the construction budget or a separate initiative. Response B specifies the months and implies these conversions are part of Phase 2 work, though it does not clarify whether they occur during or before the hospital completion work.

divergences.location: How the hospital's concerns are addressed before construction begins
divergences.response_a: Proposes forming "a joint task force with the hospital's emergency director" and funding "a third-party traffic simulation." It also offers "a legally binding memorandum of understanding (MOU) that if ambulance response times increase by more than 30 seconds post-construction, the city will allow ambulances to route through the protected bike lanes during life-or-death emergencies."
divergences.response_b: Proposes running "a micro-simulation traffic model specifically showing ambulance travel times" and presenting "this data directly to the medical director." It predicts that "once they see that a dedicated lane guarantees a clear path to the ER, they are likely to become an advocate for the redesign rather than an opponent."
divergences.nature: Response A offers a contractual safeguard (the MOU with a 30-second threshold and contingency access to bike lanes). Response B offers persuasion through data and prediction of attitude change, without proposing a contractual mechanism.
divergences.specificity: Response A specifies a measurable threshold (30 seconds) and a concrete remedy (bike lane access). Response B specifies the type of analysis (micro-simulation) but does not propose what happens if the data does not persuade the medical director or if response times do worsen post-construction.

divergences.location: How traffic demand management is framed and timed
divergences.response_a: Describes a "Know Before You Go" campaign to route through-traffic to parallel arterials, paired with Transit Signal Priority to make the bus "highly efficient, traffic-bypassing." It frames this as a reactive response to the 40% throughput drop, with the bus absorbing displaced trips as "driving becomes less convenient in Year 1."
divergences.response_b: Describes a "robust Traffic Demand Management (TDM) strategy" that begins "six months before construction" and includes telecommuting encouragement, transit pass subsidies, and dynamic signage. It frames this as proactive management to "bridge the gap to Year 3, when induced demand modelling shows traffic will naturally stabilize."
divergences.nature: Response A treats traffic management as something that happens during construction, responding to the inconvenience of driving. Response B treats traffic management as something that must begin before construction, preparing users and employers in advance.
divergences.specificity: Response A specifies the campaign name and mechanism (routing to parallel roads, bus efficiency) but does not specify when the campaign launches or how long it runs. Response B specifies the timing (six months pre-construction), the duration (through Year 3), and multiple intervention types (employer coordination, subsidies, signage), but does not name specific campaigns or specify which employers or transit agencies are involved.

divergences.location: Treatment of the equity investment in Zone 1
divergences.response_a: Describes allocating "a disproportionate amount of the $14M budget's 'soft' costs" to Zone 1, including "high-quality streetscaping, pedestrian-scale lighting, bioswales, and street trees." It also proposes "local hiring requirements" in construction contracts to ensure "direct economic benefits to the neighborhood."
divergences.response_b: Describes Zone 1 receiving "the highest-quality materials within the $14M budget," including "raised pedestrian crossings, bioswales, upgraded street lighting, and transit shelters with real-time arrival boards." It also proposes "ring-fencing" a portion of the budget explicitly for Zone 1 "so cost overruns elsewhere do not dilute their reparative investment."
divergences.nature: Response A emphasizes the composition of the investment (soft costs, local hiring) and the mechanism (disproportionate allocation). Response B emphasizes the protection of the investment (ring-fencing) and the quality of materials (raised crossings, real-time boards).
divergences.specificity: Response A specifies that soft costs are disproportionately allocated and that hiring requirements are contractual, but does not specify what percentage of the budget goes to Zone 1 or how local hiring is enforced. Response B specifies that a portion is ring-fenced but does not specify the percentage or mechanism for enforcement; it also specifies particular amenities (real-time boards) that Response A does not mention.

divergences.location: How the business support program is framed
divergences.response_a: Proposes a "Business Survival Grant" to help "ground-floor businesses with marketing or minor operational costs during the physical construction phase." It also emphasizes "case studies showing that wider ADA sidewalks and protected bike lanes frequently *increase* retail foot traffic, offsetting the perceived loss of drive-up customers."
divergences.response_b: Proposes a "Business Survival Grant program or a localized marketing campaign ('Open During Construction')." It also emphasizes "clear wayfinding signage directing customers to the newly created side-street parking."
divergences.nature: Response A frames the program as financial support plus evidence of long-term benefit. Response B frames the program as financial support plus navigation assistance during disruption.
divergences.specificity: Response A specifies the grant covers "marketing or minor operational costs" and references external evidence (case studies). Response B leaves the grant's scope open ("or a localized marketing campaign") and focuses on wayfinding as the key tool, but does not specify what the wayfinding says or where it is placed.

divergences.location: Whether the hospital zone's full completion is scheduled before or after the election
divergences.response_a: Schedules hospital construction to occur in Months 11–18, which means the zone is not fully complete until Month 18, well after the 14-month election.
divergences.response_b: Schedules the hospital's BRT/Emergency lanes to be complete by Month 12 (before the election) and the remaining work (sidewalks and bike lanes) to be complete by Month 20 (after the election).
divergences.nature: Response A keeps the entire hospital zone's construction outside the election window. Response B splits the hospital zone's work, placing the most visible and politically significant element (the emergency lanes) before the election and the remaining elements after.
divergences.specificity: Response A does not explain why the hospital zone must wait until after the election. Response B explicitly states that completing the emergency lanes before the election demonstrates "project viability" and "building trust," while deferring other work keeps "heavy construction out of the commercial district during the election cycle."
